Citations only -- no reading text is stored here; it resolves live from scripture_verse for whichever translation is current, the same citation-now/text-at-render-time split character.verse_refs already uses. 'reflection' is null for every day for now -- original devotional prose, authored separately, English first. KNOWN GAPS (small, documented, not fixed here): the lectionary's citations follow NAB/Hebrew-continuous numbering, which differs from this app's bundled WEB text for a few books -- most psalms with a sung heading run exactly one verse past WEB's real last verse (NAB counts the heading as verse 1, WEB doesn't); this app's own verse lookup already only returns verses that exist, so these just truncate one verse short rather than error. Malachi's chapter-3/4 split is corrected in the parser. Not corrected, left as a shorter-than-cited reading on those specific days: Mar 10 and May 31 (Daniel 3's Prayer of Azariah/Song of the Three Youths -- this app's bundled Daniel is the 12-chapter Hebrew canon only, missing that deuterocanonical expansion of chapter 3), Mar 23 (Daniel 13, Susanna -- same gap, an entire missing deuterocanonical chapter), Mar 14 (Psalm 51's unusually long two-line heading), Dec 12 (Zechariah 2's chapter-boundary differs between Hebrew and Greek/Vulgate numbering), and Dec 20 (Romans 16:25-27's doxology sits at a different position in some manuscript traditions than this bundled edition places it). Fixing these for real means importing the missing Daniel deuterocanonical text -- a separate scripture-import task, not a citation-parsing one. Covers through Dec 31, 2026; v3 extends through 2027.

days.reflection: The shepherds go and tell everyone what they've seen; Mary's response is different -- she keeps these things and ponders them in her heart. Both responses to God's action are real and needed: the world needs people who proclaim what they've witnessed, and it needs people who sit quietly with it long enough to let it change them. On this first day of the year, Mary's stillness is worth imitating before rushing to speak. Even his name, Jesus, given eight days after his birth just as the law required, was itself a message: "God saves." Whatever this new year holds, it begins with that same name spoken over it.

Asked directly who he is, John the Baptist starts by saying what he is not: not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet. Only after clearing that away does he give his real answer -- a voice, pointing at someone else. There's something freeing in his example: he doesn't need to be the answer to every question people bring him, only faithful to the one question he's actually been sent to answer. The first letter of John makes the point from the other side -- anyone who tries to make Jesus into something less than who he actually is has missed the whole point. Knowing clearly who you are not can be as important as knowing who you are.

John the Baptist doesn't ask his followers to look at him -- he points past himself and says, "Behold, the Lamb of God." That single line reframes everything: the one being pointed to is about to carry away the sin of the world, not just teach about it. John admits he didn't recognize Jesus himself until the Spirit showed him -- even the greatest prophet needed a sign to see what was standing in front of him. The first letter of John picks up the same thread: we are already children of God, though what we'll become isn't fully revealed yet. Like John at the Jordan, we don't always recognize grace the moment it arrives -- but that doesn't mean it isn't already here.

The Magi are outsiders in every sense -- foreign, guided by nothing more reliable than a star -- and yet they're the ones who travel the farthest to find Jesus and the ones who actually kneel down and worship him. Herod and "all Jerusalem" hear the same news and respond with fear instead. Isaiah had already promised centuries earlier that nations, not just Israel, would come to this light; Paul tells the Ephesians the promise has now visibly arrived; the Magi are proof it wasn't just poetry. It's worth asking which reaction is more natural for us: Herod's threatened grip on what he has, or the Magi's willingness to travel a long way toward something they don't yet fully understand. Epiphany means the good news was never meant to stay local.

Matthew is careful to note that Jesus didn't set up in Jerusalem, the obvious capital of religious life, but in Galilee -- a region so ordinary it gets called "Galilee of the Gentiles." That's exactly the region Isaiah had promised would see a great light, generations before it happened. John's letter warns that not every voice claiming to speak for God actually does -- the Spirit of God is recognizable by whether it acknowledges Jesus, not by how impressive it sounds. Jesus' first move as he starts his public ministry is toward the overlooked corner of the map, not the center of power. Wherever ordinary and overlooked feels like where you are, that's exactly where this Gospel begins.

The disciples' first instinct, faced with a hungry crowd and no supplies, is to send everyone away to fend for themselves. Jesus' answer cuts straight past the logistics problem: "You give them something to eat." He then takes the little they do have, blesses it, and it turns out to be enough for everyone, with baskets left over. John's letter names the source of that abundance plainly: God is love, and love isn't rationed the way we assume resources have to be. When what we have feels too small for the need in front of us, this is a strange but real invitation to bring it forward anyway.

The disciples are straining at the oars against a contrary wind when Jesus comes to them walking on the sea -- and their first reaction to seeing him is terror, mistaking him for a ghost. It takes his voice, "Take heart, it is I, don't be afraid," to turn their fear into something else. John's letter, read the same day, names exactly what was missing in that boat: "perfect love casts out fear." The disciples' fear wasn't really about the water -- it was about not yet trusting who was walking on it. Whatever wind is currently working against you, the same voice that calmed that sea is not absent from your boat either.

Jesus stands up in his hometown synagogue, reads Isaiah's words about good news for the poor and freedom for captives, and then says the line that changes everything: "Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing." He isn't just explaining an old prophecy -- he's telling people who watched him grow up that he is the one it was written about. John's letter, read the same day, insists that love for God is inseparable from love for the people right in front of us -- the same people Jesus names as the poor, the captive, the blind. It would have been easier for Nazareth to hear this from a stranger than from Joseph's son. Recognizing God at work in the familiar and the ordinary is often harder than recognizing him in the extraordinary.

The leper doesn't ask Jesus whether he's able to heal him -- he already assumes the power is there. His real question is whether Jesus wants to: "Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean." Jesus' answer removes all doubt: "I want to. Be made clean" -- immediate, no hesitation, no conditions. John's letter says God has given testimony about his Son, and whoever believes has that testimony in himself -- the same confidence the leper showed in reaching out. The harder question for most of us isn't whether God is powerful enough to help; it's whether we believe he's actually willing to.

John the Baptist's own disciples come to him worried: everyone is going to Jesus now instead of to him. His response has no trace of wounded pride in it -- he compares himself to the friend of the bridegroom, whose whole joy is simply hearing the bridegroom's voice, not competing with him. John's letter promises that whatever we ask according to God's will, he hears us; John the Baptist's own prayer, in effect, was already being answered by his own willingness to decrease. Not every calling is to be the main character in the story. There's a real, complete joy available in being the friend who's just glad to hear the voice.

John hesitates to baptize Jesus -- it should be the other way around, he says -- but Jesus insists, so it is right to fulfill all righteousness. The moment he comes up from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice names him: "You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Isaiah had described this servant centuries earlier -- gentle enough not to break a bruised reed, yet bringing justice without failing or growing discouraged. Peter later tells Cornelius's household that this is the moment it all became visible: God anointing Jesus "with the Holy Spirit and with power." The voice that named Jesus beloved before he had done a single public act of ministry is the same voice that named each of us at our own baptism.

Hannah's story starts in a very ordinary kind of grief -- provoked year after year by a rival for something she doesn't have, while everyone around her seems to have an answer except her. Simon and Andrew, James and John, are living an equally ordinary life, mending nets, when Jesus simply says, "Come after me," and they leave everything immediately. Neither Hannah's answered prayer nor the disciples' calling has actually happened yet in today's readings -- we're only at the beginning of both stories. It's worth remembering, in whatever waiting season you're in, that scripture spends real time on the "before," not just the resolution. God is already at work in a story before its turning point becomes visible.

Hannah prays so fervently, moving her lips without making a sound, that the priest Eli assumes she's drunk -- a small, painful misunderstanding on top of her grief. Jesus, teaching in the Capernaum synagogue, is recognized immediately and correctly by an unclean spirit no one else can see: "I know who you are, the Holy One of God." The contrast is striking -- a devout woman is misread by a priest, while a demon rightly names Jesus on sight. What matters in both stories isn't who understands correctly in the moment, but what happens next: Eli eventually blesses Hannah's prayer, and Jesus silences and casts out the spirit regardless of its correct answer. Being misunderstood doesn't mean you're wrong, and correctly naming Jesus isn't the same as actually following him.

Samuel hears his name called three times before Eli realizes it's the LORD calling the boy, and teaches him how to answer: "Speak, LORD, for your servant hears." Jesus, after a full evening healing the sick and casting out demons, gets up long before daylight to go to a solitary place and pray -- even he doesn't skip this. Both readings quietly insist that hearing God takes practice and quiet, whether you're a child who doesn't yet recognize the voice or the Son of God himself. If Jesus needed that early, solitary time before facing the day's demands, it isn't a luxury for the rest of us either.

Israel loses a battle, and their fix is to bring the Ark of the Covenant into camp like a good-luck charm rather than turning back to God in genuine repentance -- and they lose again, worse. The leper in Mark's Gospel does something very different: instead of demanding or assuming, he kneels and says, "If you want to, you can make me clean," leaving the real decision with Jesus. Treating something holy as a guarantee of the outcome we want is an old temptation, older than today's readings that name it. Real faith looks less like the army's presumption and more like the leper's open-handed request.

Israel demands a king "like all the nations," and God tells Samuel plainly: they have not rejected Samuel, they have rejected God. Centuries later, four friends refuse to let a crowd or a roof stop them from bringing a paralyzed man to Jesus -- and Jesus responds first not to his legs but to something deeper: "Your sins are forgiven." Israel wanted a visible king to solve a problem only God could actually fix; the paralytic's friends brought him to the one person who actually could. It's a useful question for any hard situation: are we asking for the fix that looks right, or bringing the need to the one who can actually address its root?

Saul is looking for lost donkeys when Samuel tells him God has chosen him to be king over Israel -- he wasn't looking for greatness, only for something ordinary that had gone missing. Levi is sitting at his tax booth, a job that made him an outcast among his own people, when Jesus simply says, "Follow me" -- and Levi gets up and follows, no résumé required. Neither man auditions for the calling he receives; both are simply where they are when it arrives. Jesus tells the scoffing Pharisees exactly why: "I came to call sinners, not the righteous." The calling rarely waits for us to become qualified first.

Isaiah's servant is told that being God's servant to Israel alone is "too light a thing" -- the calling is bigger: "a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth." John the Baptist points to that same widening light when he calls Jesus "the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" -- not just Israel's sin, but the world's. Paul's opening greeting to the Corinthians makes it concrete: an ordinary, mixed church in a Greek port city, already called saints, already reached by a promise that started with one nation. What began narrow in Isaiah's time has never stopped widening. Whatever feels too small or too local to matter might be exactly where that light is currently landing.

Saul keeps the best of the plunder to sacrifice to the LORD, technically religious, entirely disobedient -- and Samuel's rebuke cuts through the excuse: "to obey is better than sacrifice." Jesus tells the Pharisees something structurally similar: new wine needs new wineskins, or both the wine and the skins are ruined. Saul tried to pour new obedience into old, self-serving habits, and it split apart. Real obedience, like new wine, needs a container actually shaped for it -- not just good intentions poured into whatever old pattern is most comfortable.

Samuel is ready to anoint Jesse's oldest, most impressive-looking son, until God stops him: "man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart." David, the overlooked youngest still out with the sheep, is the one chosen. Jesus makes a related point about the Sabbath: it "was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" -- a rule meant to serve people, twisted by the Pharisees into something people are made to serve instead. Both readings push back on judging by the obvious, external measure -- of a person, or of a religious rule's actual purpose. What looks least likely, on the surface, is often exactly where God is already at work.

David faces Goliath with nothing but a sling and the conviction that the LORD, who delivered him from the paw of the lion and the bear, will deliver him from this Philistine too. Jesus, facing a hostile audience watching to see if he'll heal on the Sabbath, doesn't back down either -- he heals the man's withered hand in full view, then grieves at the hardness of heart that would rather see him fail than see a man restored. Both readings show courage that doesn't wait for the odds to look favorable. Goliath was bigger; the Pharisees' hostility was real; neither stopped the act of faith in front of them.

A simple victory song -- "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands" -- is enough to turn Saul's admiration for David into murderous jealousy. Jesus, meanwhile, draws crowds precisely because of what he does for people, healing so many that they press in just to touch him. The difference is instructive: David's growing reputation cost him nothing he did wrong, yet it still nearly cost him his life at Saul's hand. Jealousy measures itself against someone else's blessing rather than against its own; it rarely asks whether the other person actually did anything wrong. Saul's story is a warning about where an unexamined comparison can lead.

David has Saul utterly in his power in that cave and does the one thing his men can't understand: he spares him, cutting only a corner of his robe, and is troubled even by that much. Jesus appoints twelve apostles the same way scripture is read today -- calling flawed, ordinary men, including Judas Iscariot, whose ending every reader already knows. Neither reading pretends the story will be simple: David's mercy doesn't end his conflict with Saul, and Jesus' choice of twelve includes the one who will betray him. Mercy and calling aren't guarantees of a clean outcome -- they're still worth choosing.

David's lament for Saul and Jonathan is striking because Saul had spent years trying to kill him -- and David still mourns him as "the beauty of Israel," refusing to celebrate his enemy's death. Jesus' own family, meanwhile, hears about his growing ministry and concludes he must be out of his mind, coming to take custody of him. Both readings show how easily people misjudge, in opposite directions -- Saul misjudged David as a threat to eliminate; Jesus' own relatives misjudge him as someone who's lost control. Grief that refuses to gloat, even over an enemy, is its own kind of integrity worth noticing today.

Paul begs the Corinthians for something surprisingly basic: unity, no divisions, no factions rallying around "I follow Paul" or "I follow Apollos" instead of Christ. Isaiah, read the same day, promised light breaking into darkness for "Galilee of the nations" -- exactly where Matthew shows Jesus beginning his ministry and calling the first disciples. A light that arrives to unite a whole region loses something when the people who receive it start splitting into competing camps. The call to follow Christ, from the very first disciples onward, was never a call to follow a faction instead.

Paul writes to Timothy with real tenderness -- remembering his tears, longing to see him, urging him to "fan into flame" the gift of God that's already in him rather than let it go dormant. Jesus, meanwhile, is accused by scribes of casting out demons by the prince of demons, and answers with plain logic: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Timothy's gift needed active fanning, not passive possession; the scribes' accusation, by contrast, was self-contradicting nonsense dressed up as an argument. Whatever gift you've been given, today's readings suggest it needs tending, not just having.

David dances before the Ark "with all his might," unconcerned with dignity, simply glad the Ark has come home. Jesus redefines family the same day: "whoever does the will of God, he is my brother, my sister, and mother" -- a family formed by obedience, not just blood. David's uninhibited joy and Jesus' wide definition of family both point the same direction: closeness to God reorders what we thought mattered most, whether that's public dignity or the boundaries of a family tree.

David wants to build God a house; God's answer, through Nathan, reverses it entirely -- instead, the LORD will make David a house, a dynasty, not a building. Jesus' parable of the sower, read the same day, describes seed landing on different kinds of soil, some of it never producing anything at all. Both readings are about what actually lasts: not the impressive structure David wanted to build, but the quiet, ongoing thing God chooses to build instead; not every seed that's sown, but the soil that actually receives it and holds on. What we plan to build for God is sometimes smaller than what God is already building through us.

David's response to God's enormous promise isn't pride but astonished humility: "Who am I, Lord GOD... that you have brought me this far?" Jesus, the same day, says a lamp isn't lit to be hidden but set on a stand -- what's given is meant to be used and to grow, not buried. David's gratitude doesn't make him hoard the promise privately; it becomes a prayer he prays out loud, in front of others. Receiving something good from God seems to come with a built-in instinct to let it be seen, not just kept.

David's affair with Bathsheba and the murder he arranges to cover it up is one of scripture's starkest falls -- a king who stayed home from battle, took what wasn't his, and then spent enormous effort hiding it. Jesus' parable, read the same day, describes the kingdom of God growing quietly, like a mustard seed, without anyone fully understanding how. The contrast is pointed: David's sin also grew secretly, compounding in the dark before it was ever named. Whatever is growing unseen in us -- toward good or toward harm -- doesn't stay small or contained forever.

Nathan tells David a story about a rich man stealing a poor man's one lamb, and David is furious -- until Nathan says four devastating words: "You are the man." David's own sin, invisible to him while he was living inside it, becomes suddenly clear from the outside. Jesus, asleep in a storm-tossed boat, wakes to his terrified disciples and calms the sea with a word, then asks them, "Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?" Both readings involve someone needing to be woken up to a truth they couldn't see on their own, whether it's a hidden sin or a faith that's smaller than the storm. Sometimes clarity, like Nathan's parable or Jesus' calm, has to come from outside us before we can see what's actually there.
